reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Effective use and design of drilled shafts requires knowledge of construction methods; construction techniques, effort, and cost are closely tied to ground conditions. The construction technique must preserve bearing material integrity and ensure structural integrity of the cast-in-place reinforced concrete foundation. Basic construction steps: (1) excavate the hole maintaining stability, (2) clean the hole and prepare for concrete, (3) place reinforcement and concrete, (4) finish the top for connection to structure. In US practice, the contractor is responsible for choosing appropriate installation methods; unwarranted interference affecting contractor's ability to prosecute the work can lead to claims. Engineers must understand construction methods to: identify suitable conditions and estimate costs/schedule; develop constructible designs; execute site investigations for construction-relevant conditions; understand limitations affecting foundation performance or nearby structures; develop specifications and inspection procedures; develop contract provisions for payment and subsurface risk. Most important construction consideration: maintaining excavation stability to avoid loosening or collapse of the bearing formation.
key_points: Four basic steps: excavate, clean, place reinforcement/concrete, finish top
Contractor chooses construction method; unwarranted interference leads to claims
Engineers must understand construction to develop constructible designs and specifications
Maintaining excavation stability is the most critical construction consideration
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft construction; design and specification development

sections.title: Overview of Construction in Dry Stable Ground Conditions
sections.body: Stable conditions may exist in strong clays or cemented soils where groundwater is low or soils have very low permeability. Dry open-hole construction is very fast and economical (example: 15-20 shafts per day in Selma Chalk). Construction records (construction log) must be maintained as excavation advances, noting soil/rock materials encountered, obstructions, and conditions differing from expectations. Log confirms design intent and documents contract pay items. Short surface casing commonly used near ground surface for stability, as a guide for tools, and as a safety barrier. Concrete: 6-8 inch slump for dry hole use; designed for self-compaction without external vibration. In dry holes, free-fall concrete placement permitted provided a centering device directs concrete down through the center of the reinforcement. Completion: contaminated concrete (laitance due to bleed water) at top must be removed. Reinforcement extended from top for column splice, or permanent casing/form left in place for below-grade splice.
key_points: Stable dry conditions: strong clays, cemented soils, low groundwater
Concrete slump: 6-8 inches for dry hole placement
Free-fall concrete permitted in dry holes with centering device to prevent hitting rebar or hole sides
Laitance at top must always be removed even in dry placements
Construction logs are required records and document contract pay items

sections.title: Use of Casing in Drilled Shaft Construction
sections.body: Steel casing installed to prevent caving/collapse, especially when aggressive tools are used into rock or hard materials. Casing can be temporary (extracted during concrete placement) or permanent (for shafts through open water or extremely soft/unstable soils). Three methods of casing installation: (1) excavate oversized hole dry, then place casing — only for soils that remain stable long enough; (2) excavate oversized hole with drilling fluid through permeable strata, place and advance casing into bearing stratum, then bail slurry inside casing and continue dry below casing — fluid inside casing must meet slurry requirements for wet construction; (3) advance casing ahead of excavation using impact/vibratory hammers or casing oscillator/rotator, then excavate within casing dry. Most casing is recovered during concrete placement. Key risks: if casing cannot be sealed into watertight formation and hole is dewatered, groundwater and soil can flow in around base forming a cavity — causes ground subsidence, surface collapse, affects adjacent structures, and may require large unexpected concrete volume. If concrete head drops when casing is pulled and cavity exists, seal can be breached allowing groundwater/slurry contamination. Rebar cage requirements with temporary casing: no out-hook bars; cage must be self-supporting under self-weight; sufficient space between bars for concrete flow. Concrete requirements: 8-10 inch slump for casing removal operations; must maintain hydrostatic head greater than external fluid pressure at all times; must retain workability until casing fully removed. Low slump causes arching (concrete moves up with casing, creating gap for soil/water ingress) or pulls cage up. Casing diameter: ADSC standard is outside diameter in 6-inch nominal increments; shaft below casing is slightly smaller than casing I.D.
key_points: Three casing installation methods: oversized dry hole, slurry starter hole + casing, drive casing ahead
Concrete slump: 8-10 inches when casing is to be removed
Concrete must maintain hydrostatic head greater than external fluid pressure during casing extraction
Low slump causes arching — concrete moves up with casing, creating gap for water/soil ingress
Cavity outside casing from dewatering attempts can cause ground subsidence and concrete loss
Shaft below casing is slightly smaller than casing I.D. — use standard 6-in. OD increment sizes
Cage must be self-supporting; no out-hook bars; sufficient space for concrete flow through cage

sections.title: Use of Drilling Fluids in Drilled Shaft Construction
sections.body: Drilling fluids counteract groundwater head pressure and provide borehole stability via differential head pressure when fluid head in hole exceeds groundwater pressure. Types: water alone; bentonite slurry (mineral); synthetic polymer slurry. 6-step wet construction process: (1) excavate maintaining positive fluid head at all times; (2) clean hole — remove loose debris from base, clean fluids of suspended materials; (3) inspect — verify base is sound and fluid is clean; (4) place reinforcement; (5) place concrete using tremie maintaining embedment ≥10 ft below rising concrete surface; (6) extract temporary casing, clean concrete top for connection. Seepage into excavation exceeding 1 inch in 5 minutes is excessive — flood hole prior to concrete placement and use tremie method. Positive fluid head requires maintaining slurry head ≥5 ft above piezometric surface; overlying cohesive soils may mask actual piezometric surface elevation. Water as drilling fluid: suitable in stable permeable rock formations; casing through unstable overburden with water in rock socket. Bentonite slurry: montmorillonite clay absorbs water, increases viscosity and unit weight; forms filter cake at borehole wall reducing permeability and containing fluid; filter cake improves excavation stability but adversely affects concrete/soil bond at interface. Polymer drilling fluids: long-chain hydrocarbon molecules increase viscosity; no filter cake formation — greater fluid loss tendency than bentonite in coarse soils; less effective in supporting coarse-grained soils; no detrimental impact on side resistance (no filter cake buildup); predominant method in North America. Concrete for wet construction: 8-10 inch slump; tremie bottom must stay ≥10 ft below rising fresh concrete surface; slurry must be cleaned per Chapter 5 criteria before concrete placement.
key_points: Fluid head must exceed groundwater head at all times; minimum excess head 5-10 ft
Seepage >1 inch in 5 minutes: flood hole and use tremie method
Bentonite: forms filter cake — better stability in coarse soils; may reduce side resistance
Polymer: no filter cake — better side resistance; less effective in coarse-grained soils; predominant in North America
Tremie bottom must remain ≥10 ft below rising concrete surface during placement
Concrete slump: 8-10 inches for wet construction
Overlying clays may mask piezometric surface — confirm groundwater levels before drilling

sections.title: Post-Grouting and Special Techniques
sections.body: Post-grouting at the base of drilled shafts can improve base resistance in granular soils by compacting and strengthening the bearing zone. Grouting is performed through grout pipes incorporated into the rebar cage or attached to the base plate. Sleeve-port tube grouting along shaft sides is rarely used in US practice. Permeation or compaction grouting of unstable strata before excavation has been used successfully in some urban projects.
key_points: Post-grouting at base improves base resistance in granular soils
Grout pipes incorporated into rebar cage or attached to base plate
Side grouting through sleeve-port tubes is rare in US practice
Detailed guidance on post-grouted drilled shafts in Appendix H
sections.applicability: Granular soils; when high base resistance is required; urban projects with unstable strata

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter provided overview of drilled shaft construction methods covering dry, casing, and slurry techniques. Stable conditions allow open-hole dry construction. Casing and drilling fluids are primary means of excavation support in unstable conditions. Contractor is responsible for method selection; engineers must understand construction to develop constructible designs, appropriate specifications, and inspect completed work.
